chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
title: Humiliation and violence on the road in the South in the Thirties
summary: He tells of a bus stop in Georgia where women were refused a restroom, a sheriff fined the band for no reason, and a beating of a black man he witnessed, saying this is why he avoided the South.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You mentioned at one time that you didn't travel much to the South, and you said there was an incident that I should ask you about.

Well, this was pretty bad. We were changing buses down somewhere, Valdosta, Georgia or somewhere. It was right out of Florida. We had to change buses to go from one state to the other. And we were coming from Florida back up. It was at midnight, and Blanche Calloway was on the bus, and a couple of the players' wives were (?) with us(?). And they wanted to go to the ladies' room. You know? And there was nobody in the gas station at that time of night; nobody in the gas station at that time of night -- except this attendant and a deputy sheriff or a sheriff, or whatever he is. And they asked to go to...you know, where the ladies room was. And they told them the woods, if they make it. I thought that was the rottenest thing I ever heard.

Anyway, we were handing things up to...cases... suitcases up to the bus driver to put them away. "Here, Joe..." His name was Joe. "Here, Joe," DING. So here we got loaded, and leaving town. At the edge of town there was a railroad crossing, and we stop at the crossing... And after we pass the railroad crossing, here comes the deputy sheriff up. He stops us and says, "You was speedin'." He says, "How could I be speeding when I just starting up the bus?" He said, "Yeah, you was speeding across that pit(?). It's going to cost you fifteen dollars, or stay in jail all night." So he got out of the bus and started talking with the guy, and the guy said...told him, said, "That's for lettin' them niggers call you Joe."

Boy, if I could have had something, I would have really done him in! I guess it's a good thing I didn't have anything. I said, "Well, this ain't no place for me to be, down here, because I'll get myself really in trouble," you know, by people being so rotten like that.
So that's why I didn't want to go down South.

Another time we were down at... I guess it would have been around the same time. Some people were... A guy was... They used to stand around the bus and see if they knew anybody on the bus getting off -- you know, people. And the guy was standing on the sidewalk, looking in. And two women

were walking around the street, and they would have had to walk around them. So this guy... Some guy comes up to them and says, "Get out the way and let those ladies by." And he said, "Oh, I'm out of the way. I'm ...(? )...(? )... They have plenty of room to go around me." He says, "I said 'Get out of the way,'" and they knocked him, hit him -- knocked his hat off! And he said, "Pick up that hat." You know? And the guy said, "Well, I didn't do nothin'. I ain't gonna pick it up right now." The guy says, "I said pick up that hat." He started whippin' on him with knuckles -- he had knuckles.

And he happened to be... Everybody was deputized down there, down at that time, was deputized to arrest any colored person. So a guy from the garage came on over and said, "Don't bother them no more." He said, "That's my nigger." [CHUCKLES] He said, "Let him alone." Oh boy, I drank a whole pint of whiskey right then. I went and found me some whiskey and drank a whole pint, because I was so..

And that's why I didn't want to ever go there. You know, until I found that they have changed now. But at that time it was terrible. That was terrible times. And that was in the Thirties, in the early Thirties, '33, 34 or 35, around in them days.
